title: Moral certainty is still true-name certainty — not weak fluctuating assent
source_text: XI. Attamen certitudo, quam moralem dicimus, non definit esse veri nominis certitudo. Nec putandum est eo nomine designari assensum aliquem infirmum, dubium atque fluctuantem: sed excludit illa prorsus dubitationem & haesitationem. Nam pondus & gravitas authoritatis illius qua nititur, & moralis evidentia signorum & indiciorum quae illam ingenerant, sufficiunt ad animum penitus suadendum, & praestandum ut constanter ac intrepide rei assentiatur, sicut manifestum est ex exemplis propositis, & aliis quae magno numero facile esset congerere.
pass_a_gloss: Yet the certainty which we call moral does not cease to be certainty of the true name. Nor is it to be thought that by that name some weak, doubtful, and fluctuating assent is designated: but it altogether excludes doubt and hesitation. For the weight and gravity of that authority on which it rests, and the moral evidence of the signs and indications which generate it, suffice to persuade the mind thoroughly, and to make it assent constantly and intrepidly to the thing — as is plain from the examples proposed, and others which it would be easy to gather in great number.
pass_b_english: Moral certainty remains veri nominis certitudo.
Not weak/doubtful/fluctuating — excludes doubt and hesitation.
Authority-weight + moral evidence of signs suffice for constant intrepid assent.
